full_text:
In a holy temple town lived a weaver named Somilaka, whose skill at the loom surpassed all rivals. He wove garments of ethereal beauty, adorned with gold thread and floral borders, which fetched enormous prices from princes and nobles. Yet despite his ceaseless labor and large earnings, poverty clung to him like a shadow: whatever gold he earned slipped through his fingers on sudden illnesses, family misfortunes, or taxes, so that he was perpetually in debt.

Other weavers in the same town, who produced coarse, clumsy cloth and worked only three hours a day, lived in two-story brick mansions, wore silks, and dined on delicacies.

Brooding upon this injustice, Somilaka wept: 'Why does fortune mock my honest industry? I will abandon this cursed city and seek wealth in foreign lands!'

Traveling to the distant capital of Vardhamana, he labored for three years and accumulated three hundred gold dinars. Tying the gold in a waistcloth, he set out for home.

Resting for the night under a banyan tree, he was awakened at midnight by two mysterious, glowing celestial figures conversing in the branches.

One figure said: 'Brother Vidhata! Why did you grant three hundred gold dinars to Somilaka? You know well that in his past lives, he performed no charity, and his karma allows him nothing beyond daily food and coarse clothing!'

The second figure replied: 'It is my duty to reward diligence with opportunity, brother; but it is your duty, as Fate, to restrict what he may enjoy.'

When Somilaka woke at dawn, his waistcloth had been untied: a wandering thief had stolen all three hundred gold dinars!

Brokenhearted, the weaver returned to Vardhamana, labored for another three years, and saved another three hundred dinars. On his journey home, he took shelter in a roadside inn, but during the night, a sudden accidental fire broke out, burning his purse to ashes.

Despairing of life, Somilaka climbed a high cliff, resolved to hang himself from a branch.

As he tied the noose, a luminous celestial voice echoed from the sky: 'Hold your hand, Somilaka! I am Fate. It is I who took your hoarded gold, for you have not the karma to hold idle wealth. Yet because of your sincere industry, I grant you a boon: ask for whatever you desire!'

Somilaka replied: 'Grant me wealth!'

The voice asked: 'What would you do with wealth you cannot enjoy?'

Somilaka reflected upon the rich misers who guard gold without peace, and upon the contented poor who sleep without fear. He said: 'Grant me sufficient food, honorable clothing, and a contented heart that accepts what is duly mine!'

The celestial voice blessed him: 'So shall it be, Mister Duly!'

Returning to his loom, Somilaka labored with cheerful peace, receiving always what was sufficient for his honor, free from the torment of greed.

Thus Vishnu Sharma taught:
"What karma has decreed for each by ancient deeds and true,
Will surely reach his open hand in its appointed due;
He who seeks more than he has sown reaps bitterness and pain,
While he who lives with grateful heart finds peace his greatest gain."
moral: What is ordained by one's own past actions will surely come to pass; do not grieve over unavoidable losses. [PT]

options: Wisdom, patience, and kind conduct lead to peace and happiness.
Acting in hasty anger without listening

options: Through thoughtful reflection, patience, and presence of mind
By shouting loudly and blaming friends

quiz.question: What memorable conclusion does this story teach readers?
options: Patience, honesty, and humility lead to lasting harmony
quiz.hint: Think about how justice and truth prevail.
